scope: India: official and legal sources on violence, discrimination and legal status of LGBTQ people. Each fact quotes text seen in the source document by the researcher. Where a primary government site could not be opened, the source name states which copy was used.

facts.claim: On 2 July 2009 the Delhi High Court declared that Section 377 IPC, insofar as it criminalises consensual sexual acts of adults in private, is violative of Articles 21, 14 and 15 of the Constitution.
facts.sourceName: Delhi High Court, Naz Foundation v. Government of NCT of Delhi (WP(C) 7455/2001), via Indian Kanoon
facts.quote: insofar it criminalises consensual sexual acts of adults in private, is violative of Articles 21

facts.claim: On 11 December 2013 the Supreme Court in Suresh Kumar Koushal v. Naz Foundation held that Section 377 IPC does not suffer from the vice of unconstitutionality and set aside the Delhi High Court declaration.
facts.sourceName: Supreme Court of India, Suresh Kumar Koushal v. Naz Foundation, via Indian Kanoon
facts.quote: Section 377 IPC does not suffer from the vice of unconstitutionality and the declaration made by the Division Bench of the High court is legally unsustainable.

facts.claim: In Koushal (2013) the Supreme Court recorded that fewer than 200 persons had been prosecuted under Section 377 IPC in more than 150 years (as per reported orders); the 2018 Navtej bench later called this a 'de minimis' rationale.
facts.unit: persons prosecuted (upper bound stated by Court; reported orders only)
facts.sourceName: Supreme Court of India, Suresh Kumar Koushal v. Naz Foundation, via Indian Kanoon
facts.quote: in last more than 150 years less than 200 persons have been prosecuted (as per the reported orders) for committing offence under Section 377 IPC

facts.claim: On 15 April 2014 the Supreme Court in NALSA v. Union of India directed that Hijras and Eunuchs, apart from the binary genders, be treated as 'third gender' for the purpose of safeguarding their rights under Part III of the Constitution.
facts.sourceName: Supreme Court of India, National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India, via Indian Kanoon
facts.quote: Hijras, Eunuchs, apart from binary gender, be treated as “third gender” for the purpose of safeguarding their rights under Part III of our Constitution

facts.claim: NALSA (2014) upheld the right of transgender persons to decide their self-identified gender and directed the Centre and States to grant legal recognition of male, female or third gender identity.
facts.sourceName: Supreme Court of India, NALSA v. Union of India, via Indian Kanoon
facts.quote: Transgender persons’ right to decide their self-identified gender is also upheld and the Centre and State Governments are directed to grant legal recognition

facts.claim: NALSA (2014) stated that insistence on sex reassignment surgery for declaring one's gender is immoral and illegal.
facts.sourceName: Supreme Court of India, NALSA v. Union of India, via Indian Kanoon
facts.quote: any insistence for SRS for declaring one’s gender is immoral and illegal.

facts.claim: NALSA (2014) directed the Centre and States to treat transgender persons as socially and educationally backward classes and extend reservation in education admissions and public appointments.
facts.sourceName: Supreme Court of India, NALSA v. Union of India, via Indian Kanoon
facts.quote: extend all kinds of reservation in cases of admission in educational institutions and for public appointments.

facts.claim: On 24 August 2017 a nine-judge Supreme Court bench in Puttaswamy v. Union of India held that the right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21.
facts.sourceName: Supreme Court of India, Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd) v. Union of India, via Indian Kanoon
facts.quote: The right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21

facts.claim: In the Puttaswamy (2017) judgment, Justice D.Y. Chandrachud wrote that sexual orientation is an essential attribute of privacy and criticised the reasoning of Koushal.
facts.sourceName: Supreme Court of India, Puttaswamy v. Union of India (opinion of D.Y. Chandrachud J.), via Indian Kanoon
facts.quote: Sexual orientation is an essential attribute of privacy.

facts.claim: On 6 September 2018 a five-judge Constitution Bench in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India held that Section 377 IPC, insofar as it criminalises consensual sexual conduct between adults of the same sex, is unconstitutional, and that Koushal stands overruled.
facts.sourceName: Supreme Court of India, Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (opinion of Dipak Misra CJI), via Indian Kanoon
facts.quote: Section 377 of the Penal Code, in so far as it criminalises consensual sexual conduct between adults of the same sex, is unconstitutional

facts.claim: Navtej (2018) declared that the decision in Koushal stands overruled.
facts.sourceName: Supreme Court of India, Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India, via Indian Kanoon
facts.quote: The decision in Koushal stands overruled.

facts.claim: Navtej (2018) stated that the reading down of Section 377 would not reopen concluded prosecutions but could be relied upon in all pending matters at trial, appellate or revisional stages; Section 377 continues to govern non-consensual acts against adults, acts against minors and bestiality.
facts.sourceName: Supreme Court of India, Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (opinion of Dipak Misra CJI), via Indian Kanoon
facts.quote: shall not, however, lead to the re- opening of any concluded prosecutions, but can certainly be relied upon in all pending matters

facts.claim: On 17 October 2023 a five-judge Constitution Bench in Supriyo @ Supriya Chakraborty v. Union of India, declined to recognise a right of queer couples to marry or to a civil union; the Chief Justice's opinion records a heading 'There is no fundamental right to marry'.
facts.sourceName: Supreme Court of India, Supriyo @ Supriya Chakraborty v. Union of India, 2023 INSC 920 (PDF)
facts.quote: There is no fundamental right to marry

facts.claim: In his concurring majority opinion in Supriyo (2023), Justice P.S. Narasimha held that a right to a civil union or abiding cohabitational relationship conferring a legally enforceable status cannot be situated within Part III of the Constitution.
facts.sourceName: Supreme Court of India, Supriyo v. Union of India, 2023 INSC 920 (opinion of P.S. Narasimha J.)
facts.quote: cannot be situated within Part III of the Constitution of India

facts.claim: In Supriyo (2023) the Court recorded the Solicitor General's assurance that the Union Government would constitute a Committee chaired by the Cabinet Secretary to define the scope of entitlements of queer couples in unions.
facts.sourceName: Supreme Court of India, Supriyo v. Union of India, 2023 INSC 920 (opinion of D.Y. Chandrachud CJI)
facts.quote: We record the assurance of the Solicitor General that the Union Government will constitute a Committee chaired by the Cabinet Secretary

facts.claim: The Chief Justice's directions in Supriyo (2023) state that the Union, State and Union Territory governments shall not discriminate against the freedom of queer persons to enter into union with benefits under law.
facts.sourceName: Supreme Court of India, Supriyo v. Union of India, 2023 INSC 920
facts.quote: shall not discriminate against the freedom of queer persons to enter into union with benefits under law

facts.claim: On 9 January 2025 a five-judge bench dismissed the review petitions against the Supriyo judgment, considered in chambers, finding no error apparent on the face of the record.
facts.sourceName: LiveLaw, 'Supreme Court Dismisses Petitions To Review Its Judgement Refusing To Recognize Same-Sex Marriages'
facts.quote: We do not find any error apparent on the record. We further find that the view expressed in both judgments are in accordance with law

facts.claim: The review bench in January 2025 consisted of Justices B.R. Gavai, Surya Kant, B.V. Nagarathna, P.S. Narasimha and Dipankar Datta; over a dozen review petitions were dismissed.
facts.unit: review petitions (more than a dozen, as reported)
facts.sourceName: The Tribune (PTI), 'No error: Supreme Court bins petitions seeking review of same-sex marriage verdict'
facts.quote: dismissing over a dozen review petitions

facts.quote: as many as 2,195 gay sex cases were registered under Section 377 in 2016, 1,347 in 2015 and 1,148 cases in 2014

facts.sourceName: The Quint (citing NCRB data)

facts.sourceName: The Quint (citing NCRB data)
facts.quote: Altogether, 4,690 cases were registered between 2014 and 2016 under Section 377

facts.claim: The ICJ reports NCRB figures of 1279 persons arrested under Section 377 in 2014 and 1491 in 2015, and that NCRB began publishing Section 377 information only in 2014.
facts.sourceName: International Commission of Jurists, 'Unnatural Offences' (2017)
facts.quote: According to the NCRB, 1279 persons in 2014 and 1491 in 2015 were arrested under section 377.

facts.claim: In a Lok Sabha reply of 25 June 2019 the Home Ministry said NCRB's published reports were available till 2016 and gave state-wise cases pending trial under Section 377 for 2014-2016 (e.g. Kerala 209, 290, 448; Maharashtra 258, 326, 442).
facts.unit: cases pending trial at year end, Section 377
facts.sourceName: Lok Sabha Unstarred Question 582 (MHA), 25 June 2019, via shashitharoor.in
facts.quote: The published reports are available till the year 2016.

facts.claim: The same 2019 reply stated it is for State Governments/UT Administrations to consider withdrawal of Section 377 cases involving consenting adults after Navtej.
facts.sourceName: Lok Sabha Unstarred Question 582 (MHA), 25 June 2019, via shashitharoor.in
facts.quote: It is for the State Governments/UT Administrations concerned to consider withdrawal of such cases, following the due process of law.

facts.claim: A 2014 Home Ministry reply, as reported by LiveLaw, said NCRB began registering Section 377 cases in 2014 and that Delhi had the most (140).
facts.sourceName: LiveLaw, 'Government does not have separate proposal to repeal or amend section 377'
facts.quote: The maximum cases under this Section were registered in Delhi (140), out of which 110 people were arrested till September.

facts.claim: On 21 December 2021 the Home Ministry told the Lok Sabha that NCRB collected data on mob lynching and hate crimes in 2017, found it unreliable because the crimes are not defined, and discontinued collection.
facts.sourceName: ThePrint, 'NCRB stopped collecting data on lynching, hate crime as it was unreliable, govt tells LS'
facts.quote: In the year 2017, NCRB collected data on cases of mob lynching, hate crimes etc. It was observed that the data was unreliable

facts.claim: In December 2022 the Home Ministry told the Rajya Sabha that NCRB does not maintain data on hate crimes because the term is not defined in the IPC.

facts.claim: The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Bill, 2019 was introduced on 19 July 2019, passed by Lok Sabha on 5 Aug 2019 and Rajya Sabha on 26 Nov 2019.
facts.sourceName: PRS Legislative Research, Bill Track 2019
facts.quote: Introduced Lok Sabha Jul 19, 2019 Passed Lok Sabha Aug 05, 2019 Passed Rajya Sabha Nov 26, 2019

facts.claim: Offences against transgender persons under the 2019 Act carry penalties of between six months and two years and a fine.
facts.sourceName: PRS Legislative Research, Bill Track 2019
facts.quote: Penalties for these offences vary between six months and two years, and a fine.

facts.claim: The 2019 Act took effect on 10 January 2020; the Rules were notified on 25 September 2020; the National Council was constituted on 21 August 2020 and the portal launched on 25 November 2020.
facts.sourceName: PIB Backgrounder, Rights of Transgender Persons in India, 19 Nov 2025
facts.quote: Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 notified on January 10, 2020

facts.claim: The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, 2026 was introduced in Lok Sabha on 13 March 2026, passed on 24 March and by Rajya Sabha on 25 March 2026.
facts.sourceName: PRS Legislative Research, Bill Track 2026
facts.quote: Introduced Lok Sabha Mar 13, 2026 Passed Lok Sabha Mar 24, 2026 Passed Rajya Sabha Mar 25, 2026

facts.claim: The 2026 Bill removes trans-man, trans-woman and genderqueer from the statutory definition, retains socio-cultural identities and intersex variations, adds 'eunuch', and excludes persons with different sexual orientations and self-perceived sexual identities.
facts.sourceName: PRS Legislative Research, Bill Summary (15 Mar 2026)
facts.quote: The Bill removes the following categories included in the Act: (i) a trans-man or trans-woman

facts.claim: Under the 2026 Bill the District Magistrate issues the identity certificate after examining the recommendation of a designated medical board headed by a Chief Medical Officer or Deputy Chief Medical Officer.
facts.sourceName: PRS Legislative Research, Issues for Consideration (24 Mar 2026)
facts.quote: The Bill adds that the District Magistrate will issue the certificate after examining the recommendation of a designated medical board.

facts.claim: The 2026 Act deleted Section 4(2) of the 2019 Act, which had stated that a recognised transgender person has a right to self-perceived gender identity.
facts.sourceName: Supreme Court Observer, case page on the challenge
facts.quote: The Act deleted Section 4(2) of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019

facts.claim: The 2026 Bill adds offences: kidnapping and causing grievous hurt to force a transgender identity (10 years to life for adult victims); forcing a person to present as transgender for begging, servitude or bonded labour (5 to 10 years for adults).
facts.sourceName: PRS Legislative Research, Bill Summary
facts.quote: imprisonment between 10 years and life and a minimum fine of two lakh rupees if the victim is an adult

facts.claim: The 2026 amendment received the President's assent on 30 March 2026 and, per Supreme Court Observer, came into force on 25 May 2026.
facts.sourceName: Supreme Court Observer, 'Challenge to the Transgender Persons Amendment Act, 2026'
facts.quote: Subsequently, the Act was notified and came into force on 25 May.

facts.claim: On 4 May 2026 a Supreme Court bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi issued notice on the challenge to the 2026 Act, declined an interim stay (the Act not yet notified) and directed listing before a three-judge bench.
facts.sourceName: Supreme Court Observer, 4 May 2026
facts.quote: The CJI and Justice Bagchi unanimously declined the stay of the Amendment Act on the ground that the law has not been notified yet.

facts.claim: On 15 June 2026 the Supreme Court issued notice on the Union's transfer petition and stayed further proceedings in High Courts on challenges to the 2026 Act.
facts.sourceName: Supreme Court Observer, journal recap
facts.quote: On 15 June, a Bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justice Mohana issued notice in this petition, passing a stay on further proceedings before all high courts.

facts.claim: On 17 August 2026 the Solicitor General told the Supreme Court that transgender identity cards already issued would continue and not be affected by the 2026 Amendment Act, pending the challenge.
facts.sourceName: LiveLaw, 17 Aug 2026
facts.quote: transgender identity cards which have already been issued will not be affected by the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Act, 2026

facts.claim: PRS's summary of the Standing Committee report (10 Nov 2023) says the BNS removes Section 377; the Committee noted omission would mean non-consensual offences against men, transgenders and bestiality go unpenalised and recommended including it.
facts.sourceName: PRS Legislative Research, Standing Committee Report Summary on the BNS 2023
facts.quote: omitting it would mean not penalising non-consensual sexual offences against men, transgenders, and bestiality.

facts.claim: The Central Government notified that the new criminal laws replacing the IPC come into force on 1 July 2024.
facts.sourceName: Verdictum, 24 Feb 2024
facts.quote: shall come into force on July 1, 2024

facts.claim: On 7 June 2021 the Madras High Court (Justice N. Anand Venkatesh) issued guidelines for a safe environment for LGBTQIA+ people, including a suggestion for action against conversion therapy.
facts.sourceName: The News Minute, 7 June 2021
facts.quote: pronounced a historic order, giving guidelines to create a safe environment for LGBTQIA+ people

facts.claim: In its 8 July 2022 order the Madras High Court directed the National Medical Commission to list conversion therapy as professional misconduct.
facts.sourceName: LiveLaw, 10 July 2022
facts.quote: directed the National Medical Commission to enlist "Conversion Therapy" as professional misconduct

facts.claim: On 2 September 2022 the NMC declared conversion therapy professional misconduct, telling the Madras High Court it had adhered to the 8 July order.
facts.sourceName: The Quint, 5 Sep 2022
facts.quote: declared the so-called 'conversion therapy' – an unscientific practice of subjecting queer people to intervention in order to “cure” them – an act of professional misconduct

facts.claim: In February 2022 the NMC told the Madras High Court that conversion therapy amounts to professional misconduct (as reported by The News Minute).
facts.sourceName: The News Minute, 22 Feb 2022
facts.quote: amounts to professional misconduct, the National Medical Commission (NMC) has told the Madras High Court

facts.claim: On 31 May 2022 the Kerala High Court allowed a habeas corpus petition of a lesbian couple, saying they should be left to live as per their informed choice.
facts.sourceName: Verdictum, 2 June 2022
facts.quote: should be left to live their lives as per their informed choice

facts.claim: In June 2020 the Uttarakhand High Court reiterated that consensual cohabitation by a same-sex couple is not illegal, while dismissing a habeas corpus plea because the woman said she was not confined (Madhu Bala v. State of Uttarakhand).
facts.sourceName: Bar & Bench, 19 June 2020
facts.quote: Same-sex couples have got a right to live together, even if not competent to enter into wedlock

facts.claim: On 5 June 2025 PTI reported a Madras High Court division bench (Justices G.R. Swaminathan and V. Lakshminarayanan) saying 'family' must be understood in an expanded sense and that same-sex couples can constitute a family.
facts.sourceName: Deccan Herald (PTI), 5 June 2025
facts.quote: the expression "family" has to be understood in an expanded sense

facts.claim: On 17 October 2025 the Supreme Court (Justices J.B. Pardiwala and R. Mahadevan) in Jane Kaushik v. Union of India found the 2019 Act and 2020 Rules had been reduced to dead letters and directed an Advisory Committee chaired by Justice Asha Menon.
facts.sourceName: Supreme Court Observer law report, Jane Kaushik v Union of India (2025 INSC 1248)
facts.quote: The Union of India and the States have exhibited a grossly apathetic attitude towards the transgender community

facts.claim: On 26 September 2023 the NHRC issued an advisory to the Centre, States and UTs on transgender welfare, noting continuing discrimination in employment, healthcare and social exclusion.
facts.sourceName: NHRC press release, 26 Sep 2023
facts.quote: they continue to grapple with discrimination at various places like employment disparities, limited access to healthcare, and exclusion from social circles

facts.claim: On 19 May 2026 the NHRC issued Advisory 2.0 on ten areas, recommending among other things inclusion of 'Intersex', 'Transmen' and 'Transwomen' in the Census and SOPs for police and prisons.
facts.sourceName: NHRC press release, 19 May 2026
facts.quote: Inclusion of distinct categories such as ‘Intersex’, ‘Transmen’ and ‘Transwomen’ in the upcoming Census of India

timeline.title: IPC Section 377 enacted
timeline.detail: Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code was enacted in 1860 and criminalised 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature'.

timeline.title: Delhi High Court reads down Section 377
timeline.detail: Naz Foundation v. Govt of NCT of Delhi: Section 377 IPC held violative of Articles 21, 14, 15 insofar as it criminalises consensual sexual acts of adults in private.

timeline.title: Supreme Court reverses Delhi High Court (Koushal)
timeline.detail: Section 377 IPC held not unconstitutional; Parliament left free to consider deleting or amending it.

timeline.title: NCRB begins publishing Section 377 data
timeline.detail: ICJ reports NCRB only began publishing information on Section 377 in 2014; 1,148 cases were recorded that year.

timeline.title: NALSA recognises transgender persons as 'third gender'
timeline.detail: Supreme Court upholds right to self-identified gender and directs legal recognition and welfare measures.

timeline.title: Rajya Sabha passes private member's Transgender Rights Bill
timeline.detail: PRS records the Rights of Transgender Persons Bill (Tiruchi Siva, 2014) passed the Rajya Sabha in 2015 but stayed pending in the Lok Sabha.

timeline.title: Government introduces Transgender Persons Bill 2016
timeline.detail: Bill examined by the Standing Committee on Social Justice (Report No. 43, 21 July 2017); both bills lapsed with the 16th Lok Sabha.

timeline.title: Puttaswamy: right to privacy a fundamental right
timeline.detail: Nine-judge bench holds privacy protected under Article 21; opinion records sexual orientation as an essential attribute of privacy.

timeline.title: Navtej Singh Johar decriminalises consensual same-sex conduct
timeline.detail: Five-judge bench holds Section 377 unconstitutional insofar as it criminalises consensual sexual conduct between adults of the same sex; Koushal overruled.

timeline.title: Transgender Persons Bill 2019 introduced
timeline.detail: Introduced in Lok Sabha; passed 5 Aug 2019 (LS) and 26 Nov 2019 (RS).

timeline.title: Transgender Persons Act 2019 comes into force
timeline.detail: Act notified as effective on 10 January 2020.

timeline.title: National Council for Transgender Persons constituted
timeline.detail: Reconstituted by notification of 16 Nov 2023.

timeline.title: Transgender Persons Rules 2020 notified
timeline.detail: Rules require Protection Cells and Welfare Boards in States.

timeline.title: National Portal for Transgender Persons launched
timeline.detail: Online certificates and ID cards; 277 certificates issued by 24 Mar 2021.

timeline.title: Madras High Court guidelines for LGBTQIA+ persons
timeline.detail: Justice N. Anand Venkatesh issues guidelines including action against conversion therapy.

timeline.title: SMILE scheme approved
timeline.detail: Standing Finance Committee approved SMILE on 30 Nov 2021; launched 12 Feb 2022.

timeline.title: Government tells Lok Sabha hate-crime data collection discontinued
timeline.detail: MHA said NCRB collected hate crime data in 2017 and stopped as it was unreliable.

timeline.title: SMILE launched
timeline.detail: Umbrella scheme with a transgender welfare sub-scheme (Garima Greh, skills, health, portal).

timeline.title: Kerala High Court reunites lesbian couple
timeline.detail: Habeas corpus petition allowed; couple left to live per informed choice.

timeline.title: NMC declares conversion therapy professional misconduct
timeline.detail: Following Madras High Court directions of 8 July 2022.

timeline.title: NHRC advisory on transgender welfare
timeline.detail: Advisory to Centre, States and UTs.

timeline.title: Supriyo v. Union of India (marriage equality)
timeline.detail: Constitution Bench declines to recognise queer marriage or civil unions; records Solicitor General's assurance of a Cabinet Secretary-led committee.

timeline.title: Standing Committee report on BNS recommends retaining Section 377-type provision
timeline.detail: Committee noted non-consensual offences against men, transgenders and bestiality would otherwise be unpenalised.

timeline.title: Cabinet Secretary committee on queer community constituted
timeline.detail: Gazette notification following the Supriyo judgment.

timeline.title: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaces IPC
timeline.detail: Section 377 has no equivalent in the BNS.

timeline.title: Review of Supriyo dismissed
timeline.detail: Five-judge bench dismisses review petitions in chambers.

timeline.title: Jane Kaushik v. Union of India
timeline.detail: Supreme Court directs Advisory Committee under Justice Asha Menon on equal-opportunity policy.

timeline.title: Transgender Amendment Bill 2026 introduced
timeline.detail: Passed LS 24 Mar, RS 25 Mar; assent 30 Mar 2026.

timeline.title: Supreme Court issues notice on challenge to 2026 Act
timeline.detail: Interim stay declined; three-judge bench to hear.

timeline.title: NHRC Advisory 2.0
timeline.detail: Recommends inclusive census categories and police/prison SOPs.

timeline.title: Centre tells Supreme Court existing ID cards continue
timeline.detail: Solicitor General statement before three-judge bench.

other._note377: No verified figure for 2017, 2018, 2019; 2024 not reported (Section 377 has no BNS equivalent). 2014-2016 via PTI/The Quint citing NCRB; 2020-2023 from NCRB Crime in India tables.

unconfirmed: NCRB Section 377 case counts for 2017, 2018 and 2019: no figure opened (a 2,187 figure for 2017 appeared only in a search summary of a secondary article and was not verified).
NCRB did not publish a 2024 'Unnatural Offences' count; the 2024 report shows a dash. No other NCRB table on transgender rape victims exists in Volume I (rape tables are titled for women and girls).

NCRB transgender victim counts for 2020 and 2021 (murder, kidnapping): earlier Crime in India volumes could not be opened; only the 2022, 2023 and 2024 volumes were read. Official ncrb.gov.in pages failed TLS verification from this environment, so PDF copies hosted by Bar & Bench (2022) and OpenCity (2023, 2024) were used.
March 2015 Lok Sabha reply that NCRB collected no separate data on transgender persons: seen only as a search summary of an eparlib.nic.in PDF that could not be opened.
Lok Sabha/Rajya Sabha Section 377 answers on MHA site (e.g. RS 28 Mar 2018 Q3742): MHA PDF links returned 404; not used.

Figures of 24,115 applications, 15,800 certificates and 3,200 pending beyond 30 days (December 2023 Lok Sabha) appear only in a Leaflet article citing the Times of India; the parliamentary text was not opened.
NCW (National Commission for Women) statements or reports on transgender persons: none found.
Delhi High Court habeas corpus orders for queer couples: none located and verified. Kerala (2022), Uttarakhand (2020) and Madras (2025, as reported by PTI) orders are included.
Section 377 prosecution counts before 2018 beyond the Koushal observation (fewer than 200 reported prosecutions in 150 years) and NCRB 2014-2016 counts: none verified.

Exact date the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Act 2026 was gazetted/notified: Supreme Court Observer says it came into force on 25 May 2026; the notification itself was not opened. Outcome of the Supreme Court challenge after the 17 August 2026 hearing was not found.

Garima Greh beneficiary numbers nationwide and year-wise release figures beyond the state table in RS Q621 (2023-24, 2024-25) were not compiled. Counts of Garima Grehs differ between sources (21 in PIB Nov 2025 and Apr 2026; 23 in RS replies of Feb 2026) because of differing dates.

The SMILE total allocation differs between PIB documents (Rs 365 crore in May 2025; Rs 390 crore in April 2026) because the beggary sub-scheme figures differ; the transgender sub-scheme figures (total Rs 265 crore) agree.
Any government statement specifically on hate crimes against LGBTQ persons: none found. Only general statements on hate-crime data (2017 collection discontinued; term not defined) were verified.
Madras High Court order date for the NMC direction: LiveLaw reports 10 July 2022 coverage; The Quint refers to an order of 8 July 2022. 8 July is used.
